        <h1>Threat Intelligence for SOC Analysts</h1>
        <div class="meta">
            <span>📖 10 min read</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Intermediate</span>
            <span>📅 Updated: November 2025</span>
        </div>
    </header>

    <div class="content">
        <p>
            Threat intelligence (TI) is one of the most powerful tools in a Security Operations Center (SOC)
            analyst's arsenal. When properly integrated into your security workflow, TI transforms reactive incident
            response into proactive threat hunting and defense. This guide will show you how to effectively leverage
            threat intelligence feeds for security operations and incident response.
        </p>

        <h2>What is Threat Intelligence?</h2>
        <p>
            Threat intelligence is evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging threats that can help you
            make informed security decisions. It includes:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)</strong> - IP addresses, domains, file hashes, URLs
                associated with malicious activity</li>
            <li><strong>Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs)</strong> - How threat actors operate</li>
            <li><strong>Threat Actor Profiles</strong> - Information about specific groups and their motivations
            </li>
            <li><strong>Vulnerability Intelligence</strong> - Information about exploited vulnerabilities</li>
            <li><strong>Contextual Information</strong> - Campaign details, attribution, and impact analysis</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>Types of Threat Intelligence</h2>

        <h3>1. Strategic Intelligence</h3>
        <p>
            High-level intelligence for executive decision-making. Includes threat landscape trends, geopolitical
            risks, and industry-specific threats. Useful for risk assessments and security strategy planning.
        </p>

        <h3>2. Tactical Intelligence</h3>
        <p>
            Information about threat actor TTPs. Helps security teams understand how attacks are conducted and how
            to detect them. Essential for threat hunting and detection engineering.
        </p>

        <h3>3. Operational Intelligence</h3>
        <p>
            Details about specific attacks, campaigns, or threat actors. Includes information about ongoing threats
            and their infrastructure. Critical for incident response and threat tracking.
        </p>

        <h3>4. Technical Intelligence</h3>
        <p>
            Specific IOCs like IP addresses, domains, file hashes, and malware signatures. Most commonly used by SOC
            analysts for detection and blocking. Directly actionable in security tools.
        </p>

        <h2>Key Threat Intelligence Feeds</h2>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Feed</th>
                    <th>Type</th>
                    <th>Best For</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>CISA KEV</td>
                    <td>Vulnerability</td>
                    <td>Patch prioritization</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>AlienVault OTX</td>
                    <td>IOCs</td>
                    <td>Community-driven threat data</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Abuse.ch</td>
                    <td>Malware</td>
                    <td>Malware hashes, C2 servers</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>OpenPhish</td>
                    <td>Phishing</td>
                    <td>Phishing URL detection</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>MISP</td>
                    <td>Multi-source</td>
                    <td>Collaborative threat sharing</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2>Integrating TI into Your SOC Workflow</h2>

        <h3>Step 1: Define Your Intelligence Requirements</h3>
        <p>
            Before consuming threat intelligence, identify what you actually need:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>What threats are most relevant to your organization?</li>
            <li>What industries or geographies do you operate in?</li>
            <li>What assets are you trying to protect?</li>
            <li>What detection capabilities do you already have?</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="highlight-box">
            <strong>Pro Tip:</strong> Don't try to consume every threat feed available. Focus on high-quality,
            relevant feeds that align with your organization's risk profile.
        </div>

        <h3>Step 2: Automate Feed Ingestion</h3>
        <p>
            Manual threat intelligence consumption doesn't scale. Automate feed ingestion into your security tools:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>SIEM Integration</strong> - Ingest IOCs for correlation with security events</li>
            <li><strong>Firewall/IPS</strong> - Block malicious IPs and domains automatically</li>
            <li><strong>EDR/XDR</strong> - Alert on file hash matches</li>
            <li><strong>Email Gateway</strong> - Block phishing URLs and malicious attachments</li>
            <li><strong>Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP)</strong> - Centralize and enrich all TI data</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Step 3: Enrich and Contextualize</h3>
        <p>
            Raw IOCs are just data points. Add context to make them actionable:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>Confidence scores (how reliable is this indicator?)</li>
            <li>Threat severity (how dangerous is this threat?)</li>
            <li>First/last seen dates (is this still active?)</li>
            <li>Associated campaigns or threat actors</li>
            <li>Recommended actions (block, alert, investigate)</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Step 4: Operationalize in Detection</h3>
        <p>
            Use threat intelligence to improve your detection capabilities:
        </p>

        <pre><code># Example: SIEM correlation rule using threat intelligence

Alert when internal host communicates with known C2 server

IF (network_connection.destination_ip IN threat_intel.malicious_ips) AND (network_connection.source_ip IN internal_networks) THEN ALERT “Potential C2 Communication Detected” SEVERITY: HIGH RECOMMENDED_ACTION: Isolate host, investigate

        <h3>Step 5: Enable Threat Hunting</h3>
        <p>
            Use TI to proactively hunt for threats in your environment:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>Search historical logs for IOCs from recent campaigns</li>
            <li>Look for TTPs associated with threat actors targeting your industry</li>
            <li>Identify anomalies that match known attack patterns</li>
            <li>Investigate suspicious activity that correlates with TI</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them</h2>

        <h3>1. Alert Fatigue from False Positives</h3>
        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong>Problem:</strong> Low-quality threat feeds generate too many false positives, overwhelming
            analysts.
            <br><br>
            <strong>Solution:</strong> Implement confidence scoring, use reputable feeds, and tune detection rules
            based on your environment.
        </div>

        <h3>2. Stale Intelligence</h3>
        <p>
            IOCs have a shelf life. An IP address that was malicious last year might now belong to a legitimate
            organization.
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>Implement TTL (time-to-live) for IOCs</li>
            <li>Regularly refresh threat feeds</li>
            <li>Remove expired indicators from blocklists</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>3. Lack of Context</h3>
        <p>
            An IP address alone doesn't tell you much. Always ask:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>Why is this indicator malicious?</li>
            <li>What campaign is it associated with?</li>
            <li>What should I do if I see it?</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>4. Over-Reliance on IOCs</h3>
        <p>
            Threat actors can easily change IOCs (new domains, IPs, file hashes). Focus on:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Behavioral detection</strong> - Detect malicious behavior, not just known indicators</li>
            <li><strong>TTP-based hunting</strong> - Look for attack techniques that are harder to change</li>
            <li><strong>Anomaly detection</strong> - Identify deviations from normal behavior</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>Practical Workflow Example</h2>

        <h3>Morning Threat Intelligence Review</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Check overnight TI alerts</strong> - Review any matches between your environment and new
                IOCs</li>
            <li><strong>Review new campaigns</strong> - Read about emerging threats relevant to your industry</li>
            <li><strong>Update detection rules</strong> - Add new TTPs to your detection logic</li>
            <li><strong>Threat hunt</strong> - Search for historical evidence of new threats</li>
            <li><strong>Share findings</strong> - Brief team on critical threats and recommended actions</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Incident Response with TI</h3>
        <p>
            When investigating an incident:
        </p>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Extract IOCs</strong> - Pull IPs, domains, hashes from the incident</li>
            <li><strong>Pivot on TI</strong> - Search threat feeds for related indicators</li>
            <li><strong>Identify campaign</strong> - Determine if this is part of a known attack</li>
            <li><strong>Understand TTPs</strong> - Learn how the threat actor operates</li>
            <li><strong>Predict next steps</strong> - Anticipate what the attacker might do next</li>
            <li><strong>Share intelligence</strong> - Contribute your findings back to the community</li>
        </ol>

        <h2>Tools for Threat Intelligence</h2>

        <h3>Free/Open Source</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>MISP</strong> - Open-source threat intelligence platform</li>
            <li><strong>OpenCTI</strong> - Cyber threat intelligence platform</li>
            <li><strong>TheHive</strong> - Security incident response platform with TI integration</li>
            <li><strong>Yeti</strong> - Platform for organizing observables and IOCs</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Commercial</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Recorded Future</strong> - Real-time threat intelligence</li>
            <li><strong>ThreatConnect</strong> - Threat intelligence platform</li>
            <li><strong>Anomali</strong> - ThreatStream platform</li>
            <li><strong>CrowdStrike Falcon Intelligence</strong> - Integrated TI with EDR</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>Measuring TI Effectiveness</h2>

        <p>
            Track these metrics to evaluate your threat intelligence program:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Detection Rate</strong> - How many threats were detected using TI?</li>
            <li><strong>Time to Detection</strong> - How quickly did TI help identify threats?</li>
            <li><strong>False Positive Rate</strong> - How many TI alerts were false positives?</li>
            <li><strong>Coverage</strong> - What percentage of your attack surface is covered by TI?</li>
            <li><strong>Actionability</strong> - What percentage of TI led to concrete actions?</li>
        </ul>

        <h2>Best Practices</h2>

        <div class="success-box">
            <ul style="margin: 0;">
                <li><strong>Start small</strong> - Begin with 2-3 high-quality feeds, expand gradually</li>
                <li><strong>Automate everything</strong> - Manual TI consumption doesn't scale</li>
                <li><strong>Add context</strong> - Raw IOCs are useless without context</li>
                <li><strong>Share intelligence</strong> - Contribute back to the community</li>
                <li><strong>Focus on TTPs</strong> - Behavioral detection beats IOC matching</li>
                <li><strong>Measure impact</strong> - Track how TI improves your security posture</li>
                <li><strong>Train your team</strong> - Ensure analysts know how to use TI effectively</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h2>Conclusion</h2>
        <p>
            Threat intelligence is not just about collecting IOCs—it's about understanding your adversaries and
            using that knowledge to defend proactively. When properly integrated into your SOC workflow, TI
            transforms security operations from reactive firefighting to strategic defense.
        </p>
        <p>
            Start with clear intelligence requirements, automate feed ingestion, enrich data with context, and
            operationalize it in your detection and response processes. Most importantly, remember that threat
            intelligence is only as valuable as the actions it enables.
        </p>

        <div class="highlight-box">
            <strong>Next Steps:</strong> Check out our <a href="/guides/openphish-integration.html">OpenPhish Feed
                Integration Guide</a> to learn how to integrate phishing intelligence into your security stack.
        </div>
    </div>
